verdicts.rewritten_summary: Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): consensual same-sex conduct legal throughout the country since 2022 — the High Court in Jamal Jeffers v The Attorney General struck Offences Against the Person Act s.56 (buggery) and s.57 (indecent assault against men) as contrary to privacy and expression rights; legal gender recognition is not possible; LGBTI organisations may register.

adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Saint Kitts and Nevis - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Country status page (fetched 2026-09-29): criminalisation of homosexuality rescinded in 2022; the penal code still contains no discrimination or harassment protections on sexual orientation or gender identity; same-sex unions are not recognised in any form (marriage or partnership), and same-sex households receive none of the rights afforded to opposite-sex married couples; gender identity recognition unavailable.

adds.title: 76crimes tag page: Saint Kitts and Nevis
adds.summary: Tag archive (fetched 2026-09-29): Saint Kitts and Nevis collection led by 'Courts are the key to expanding LGBTQ rights in the Caribbean' and 'Lawsuits target 5 Caribbean nations' anti-gay laws' — advocacy coverage of the region's court-driven anti-sodomy-law challenges; the site tracks 66+ countries' anti-gay laws and reports no post-repeal discrimination statute for Saint Kitts and Nevis.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Seoul Central District Court, final 2 Jul 2024 (no appeal): police advising a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights; symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state, recognising the infringement.

Yonhap (8 May 2024): a court (Yeongdong) ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery to change legal sex status — five plaintiffs assigned male at birth, on hormone therapy for years; the court held demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals.

The Hankyoreh (21 Mar 2024): youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong research presented 20 Mar 2024 shows trans teens avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed — a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reports holding it in and leaving school early; researchers urged law and institutional reforms for safer school environments.

Korea Herald (28 Nov 2023): the state human rights watchdog NHRCK flagged a 'transgender blind spot in hospitalisation' — the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): civilian same-sex conduct legal but criminalised in the military under Military Criminal Act Art. 92-6, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023; legal gender recognition possible; no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity; LGBTI organisations can register.

Peer-reviewed nationwide survey (Epidemiology and Health, 27 Jun 2025): 585 transgender and non-binary young adults mapped key milestones and stigmatization across life stages — documents pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care.

HRW World Report 2025, South Korea chapter (events of 2024): overall relatively positive record with free media and civil society, but persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people; chapter also covers the December 2024 martial-law crisis and assembly freedoms.

HRW (4 Aug 2017, 'South Korea: Supreme Court Affirms LGBT Rights'): documents LGBT registration litigation — an NGO won at Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017, with the government appealing to the Seoul High Court and Supreme Court; HRW criticises years of bureaucratic obstruction of LGBT group registration.

HRW (16 Jan 2008): Kuwait's National Assembly added Article 199 bis to Penal Code Art. 198 — 'indecent act in a public place, or imitating the appearance of a member of the opposite sex' punishable by up to 1 year imprisonment or a 1,000-dinar (US$3,500) fine; the only known targets of the law were transgender people, who can neither change legal documents nor find protection from such policing.

HRW (17 Feb 2022): Kuwait's Constitutional Court struck down the 2007 anti-transgender provision ('imitating the opposite sex') as unconstitutional; HRW urged parliament to repeal the law outright — the ruling removed criminal exposure but not the underlying dress-code policing practice.

US State Dept 2023 Country Report on Kuwait (via ecoi): communications regulator CITRA blocked LGBTQI+ material including advocacy and legal information; no candidate ran for National Assembly openly acknowledging LGBTQI+ orientation — documents censorship and invisibility of LGBT political participation.

HRW World Report 2024, Kuwait (events of 2023): penal code art. 193 still punishes consensual same-sex relations between men by up to 7 years and adultery by up to 5 years; positive step noted — Feb 2022 Constitutional Court ruling unconstitutional the 2007 art. 198 'imitating' provision.

Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute (11 Jul 2024): the 2007 amendment criminalising 'imitating the opposite sex' was proposed by MP Waleed Al-Tabtabaei with overwhelming parliamentary support, and abolished by the Constitutional Court in 2022 after an individual targeted by police challenged it — analysis of the steps still needed after abolition.

DAWN MENA (13 Feb 2023, Nora Noralla): a year after the Constitutional Court overturned the anti-transgender law, transgender discrimination continues in practice — the ruling was not a first step toward recognizing transgender rights, with social and employment discrimination persisting.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' (16 Apr 2018): regional study of LGBT activism in 22 MENA jurisdictions incl. Kuwait, based on interviews with 34 activists; six interviewees from Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman, Syria and Morocco had relocated to Europe for security reasons tied to their identity or activism.

Human Dignity Trust history: Laos (with Cambodia) achieved independence from France in the 1950s and modelled its penal code on the French system — it has never formally criminalised same-sex conduct, distinguishing it from neighbours that retained colonial sodomy offences.

GlobalGayz first-person account (2000, Richard Ammon): during a week in Vientiane the writer met a small circle of lesbians and gay men whose lives centred on a few restaurants and friendship networks — the country's LGBT scene is small, discreet and social rather than public or institutional.

Al Jazeera in-depth (Oct 2018): government crackdown on social media — influential Facebook users ('net idols') face retribution for posts, and 'Proud to be us Laos', the country's only LGBT advocacy group, is quoted; indicates online LGBT expression operates under tightening state attention.

EEAS page (title-verified; body behind JavaScript wall): the EU celebrated International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia in Vientiane — diplomatic visibility for LGBT rights; no further detail retrievable.

Cairo 52 country review: Lebanon employs both de facto and explicit criminalisation to penalise transgender expression, particularly targeting transgender women; a rise in prejudice and violence against trans and queer people is documented in Beirut, including incidents responding to a decriminalisation bill tabled in parliament; gradual legal-gender-recognition progress since 2015 when a judge approved a plaintiff's gender-marker change on identity documents.

EUAA Country Focus Lebanon sec. 7.5 (fetched 2026-09-29): dedicated section on LGBTIQ persons including activists in the asylum country-of-origin report — treats LGBTIQ claims as a distinct risk category with defined terms of reference and source methodology.

HRW (8 Apr 2022, Nora Noralla): regional dispatch 'Tough Territory for Transgender People' — Egypt, Lebanon and Tunisia should ensure access to legal gender recognition; documents trans people's exposure to policing and documentation barriers in Lebanon alongside neighbours.

Manara Magazine (Mar 2022, Nora Noralla): maps MENA case law on legal gender recognition — the Lebanese judiciary has a long history of reviewing trans plaintiffs' name/marker changes governed by the civil registry code of 1951, with an 1887-era... [Lebanese Civil Decision 1987] precedent and heavy roles for medical and religious authorities; compares Lebanon with Egypt, Kuwait and UAE reasoning.

Outright country overview (updated Mar 2026), at-a-glance: same-sex relations for men and for women are not legal throughout the country; legal gender recognition not possible (overview page cached truncated at ~5KB; article-level detail on Art. 534 not retrievable in cache).

HRW (18 May 2018): security forces arrested a prominent LGBT rights activist and pressured him to cancel Beirut Pride — nine days of LGBT-identity activities — in a crackdown HRW called a violation of freedom of assembly and a step backward for LGBT rights.

The Daily Beast (15 May 2018): profile of Georges Azzi, who co-founded Helem in 2004 (the first LGBT advocacy group in the Arab world) and later led the Arab Foundation for Freedoms and Equality, campaigning for LGBT equality across hostile regional countries.

HRW (2 Feb 2017): 'Another Judge Questions Legal Basis of Prosecuting Homosexivity Under Lebanese Law' — a ruling pushed Lebanon closer to decriminalising same-sex conduct, following the 2009 precedent that consensual same-sex conduct is not a criminal offence.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 Oct 2024): Rep. Johnson N. Williams is seeking lawmakers' support for a harsh anti-homosexuality bill filed that summer; related proposals would imprison children as young as 10 years old for gay sex — documents active legislative threat beyond the existing statute.

NPR (9 Apr 2012, 'Liberian LGBT Rights Under Spotlight'): anti-gay sentiment growing since the US announced plans to promote LGBT rights overseas; new legislation proposed longer jail time for homosexuality and a group distributed fliers targeting gay-rights supporters.

The Guardian (19 Mar 2012, Monrovia): Nobel Peace Prize president Ellen Johnson Sirleaf defended laws criminalising homosexuality in a joint interview; her remarks drew international comment on Liberia's stance (Blair declined to comment).

Cairo 52 country review: Libya has de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and of the transition process (social, medical, surgical), enforced through 'indecent acts' and 'illicit intercourse' provisions; recent religious rulings have designated gender-affirming medical steps as impermissible.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations not legal for men or women; 'indecent acts' provisions carry up to 5 years' imprisonment; no legal protections against SOGI discrimination; same-sex relationships not legally recognised; legal gender recognition unavailable (official identity documents cannot be changed); LGBTI organisations cannot register.

The Guardian, Brian Whitaker guide (21 Jun 2016): Libya is among regional states where homosexuality carries imprisonment as the penalty (specific terms vary by country); where no specific law exists, other laws are used — the guide assesses the catastrophic effect of these regimes on gay people's lives.

HRW (8 Jun 2015): documents Islamic State's killing of men accused of homosexuality in territory it controlled, including Derna, Libya — a young man there was targeted by local Islamists for effeminate dress and 'contemporary' clothes (case named from Nov 2014).

D+C (Jun 2015): Islamist extremists executed three young men accused of homosexual acts in Derna in April 2015; the piece reports information in Derna flows only through the mosque and concludes the situation for homosexuals in Libya is getting worse as militias control territory.
HuffPost (26 Nov 2012): 12 men accused of being gay faced torture and threatened death at the hands of a Libyan militia — early post-revolutionary vigilante violence against suspected gay men.

HRW (31 Jul 2025): the Saint Lucia High Court decriminalized same-sex conduct — struck down the criminal provision as unconstitutional (Eastern Caribbean strategic litigation); visitor-facing criminal exposure for consensual same-sex conduct ended.

Erasing 76 Crimes (4 Apr 2017): Caribbean LGBTI activists — United and Strong of St Lucia and ECADE — protested a PinkNews item (28 Mar 2017) framing regional sexuality, under the banner 'Nothing about us without us'; documents regional civil-society pushback against outsider framing of Caribbean LGBT issues.

United and Strong St Lucia (21 May 2015): human-rights sensitisation training for law enforcement held Castries 19 May 2015 — officers from RSLPF, Air and Sea Ports, Customs and Bordelais Correctional facility, with CariFLAGS, the Canadian HIV-AIDS Legal Network and Maurice Tomlinson; builds on 2014 sensitisation work.

UNSW human-rights review of anti-trans violence in Indonesia: documents that in November 2018 three transwomen were raided by Satpol PP (the regional morals-and-order force) in Lampung province — detained at the Satpol PP office and hosed down at the firefighter building, with an officer recording it — alongside a national pattern of transwomen murdered in 2017 (Bone, Semarang, South Sulawesi) and election-cycle anti-LGBT bylaw lobbying from 2016 onward; an SMRC survey of 1,520 Indonesians (Nov 2016) found LGBT people hated by 16.6%.

OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation study analyses discriminatory regional regulations in eight Indonesian provinces — Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatera, South Sulawesi, South Sumatera and Yogyakarta — at province and district level; Lampung is named among them, supporting this record's claim of discriminatory regional regulation. (Text recovered by partial PDF extraction; cached file is a truncated PDF.)

Asia-Pacific Solidarity Network report (22 Jul 2025): police and military in Maybrat and the Central Highlands areas of West Papua committed 138 recorded acts of torture or other ill-treatment against people in detention (period through early 2025); most victims male under 24, seven female, seven minors aged 15-17, with near-total impunity — 'impunity, secrecy and silence'. Direct security-force risk context for any visitor to the province.

Papua human-rights monitor quarterly, Q3 2025: notable increase in military deployments and operations in West Papua's highland regions since August 2025; in Sorong police arrested over a dozen protest participants (Aug 2025); on 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in Agats, Asmat Regency; ongoing displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous Papuans. No trans-specific findings — risk relevance is the general security-force pattern amplifying exposure for any visibly gender-nonconforming visitor.

OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation study covers eight provinces — Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatera, South Sulawesi, South Sumatera, Yogyakarta; Central Kalimantan is NOT among them, so this page yields no direct finding for this province: thin: no usable finding. Its use here is scope-exclusion evidence supporting the record's no-subnational-signal claim.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation study lists North Sumatera among the eight provinces whose regional regulations it analysed as discriminatory toward women and LGBTIQ people, describing the province as volatile and multi-ethnic; regulations examined at province and district level. Supports the record's legal-divergence signal; no enforcement incident appears in this source.

No direct finding for this province: thin: no usable finding; retained as scope-exclusion evidence for the record's no-signal claim.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation study names Yogyakarta (Jogjakarta) among the eight provinces whose regional regulations it analysed as discriminatory toward women and LGBTIQ people, alongside DKI Jakarta, Aceh and others; regulations operate at province and district level. Supports this record's legal-divergence signal; the source documents no specific enforcement incident for the province.

University of KwaZulu-Natal (Durban) Masters criminology thesis, 2024 (Buthelezi, Ayanda Nomfundo): 'A criminological exploration of queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minority in KwaMashu Township' — 15 queer participants purposively sampled from the Imvelo Yesizwe Organisation, in-depth interviews; findings report significant victimisation of queer individuals in township settings and examine adequacy of support/interventions and safety strategies.

PinkNews (26 Jan 2012): Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival prompted demands for apology; police opened investigation, with the KwaZulu-Natal Premier and Contralesa weighing in on the royal family's account. Region-specific evidence of top traditional authority hostility toward gay people in the province.
